excerpt: Duku is a registered lanzones variety. The Philippine Seed Board approved it in 1991. Davao NCRDC bred it.

blocks.text: Its seller and farm sources add notes, listed at the end. Compare it with the others in our [lanzones variety finder](/crop-varieties/lanzones), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [Land preparation for fruit trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).
When does it bear, and how much?

A registered tree variety is described from its mother tree, not from trial plots. The mother tree of Duku was about 10 meters tall when it was registered. A grafted or marcotted tree bears years sooner than one grown from seed, and its yield climbs as the tree grows.

anee.io keeps the records of each block of trees, from fertilizer to harvest, with [the growth stages and weather](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) beside them.
Is it resistant to pests and diseases?
No pest or disease ratings are published for this variety. So treat it as untested, and scout every week.
The pests and diseases that hit lanzones fields most often: [mealybug](/pests/mealybug). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.
A fruit of Duku weighs about 16.79 grams, and its shape is obovoid. The flesh is smooth and firm. The edible part is 76.08 percent of the fruit.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Fruit:** Bunches of 4 to 12, round fruit about 17 g, thicker skin with little or no latex when ripe, 1 to 2 seeds, about 18 Brix, about 76 percent edible.
Registered in 1991 with the Philippine Seed Board.

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: commercially grown big, round lanzones with little latex. Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant Duku lanzones

Paete and Camiguin lanzones are prized for sweet, seedless segments. Plant grafted trees, which bear years sooner than seedlings. A registered tree variety is a selection from one proven mother tree, and only grafted, budded or marcotted plants carry its traits. A seedling grown from its seed can turn out quite different. So buy from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, and ask which mother tree the scions came from. Before planting, get the field ready with our guide: [Pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).

items: Buy grafted or budded plants from an accredited nursery, with the variety name on the tag.
Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Plant a few trees first if the variety is new to your area, before you fill the whole farm.
Write down the planting day, inputs and harvest, so you can compare varieties on your own ground. anee.io keeps these records for you.
